title: Neural Networks in Trading: A Spike-Semantic Approach to Spatiotemporal Identification (Conclusion)
text:
Introduction
Just because the market is quiet does not mean it is calm. Beneath its smooth surface, life is constantly bubbling: bursts of orders, tremors in liquidity, and shifts in trading volume. All of this consists of brief, almost imperceptible impulses that give rise to price movements. Every tick is a signal in the living fabric of the market. And it is precisely in those moments, when most people still see only silence, that the real process of trend formation begins.
Traditional methods of analysis are too slow to capture this moment. They see only a fait accompli — a candlestick, an extremum, a pattern. But what matters to a trader is something else: sensing a change before it becomes obvious. And this is where the new generation of models comes in — architectures capable of recognizing
events
.
One such architecture is
S3CE-Net
—
Spike-guided Spatiotemporal Semantic Coupling and Expansion Network
. It was originally designed to process data streams from event cameras, where each pixel captures not a static image but an instantaneous change in light — a sort of
spike
or
pulse
. Essentially, these are the same events as those in the market: irregular, asynchronous, brief, yet significant.
We wondered: after all, the financial market is an event-driven system too. Time does not flow uniformly here. Everything is determined by bursts of activity — moments when a major player suddenly appears in the order flow, liquidity tightens, and the price accelerates. If we teach the model to perceive these impulses as a
structure
, it will be able to anticipate and react.
In previous articles, we have already explored the theoretical foundation of the
S3CE-Net
framework. We considered the concept of the event-driven approach, explained why the market can be viewed as a stream of impulses, and laid the groundwork for implementing the proposed approaches in the
MQL5
environment.
The next stage was an engineering step forward: we implemented the
SSAM
(
Spike-guided Spatial-Temporal Attention Mechanism
) module and adapted it to the computational characteristics of the trading terminal.
Now it is time for the final stage. Here, we bring everything together — from concept to practice, from event theory to evaluating the results. We will examine how
S3CE-Net
behaves on real historical data, how resilient it is to market noise, and whether its attention can distinguish true signals from random fluctuations.
The
S3CE-Net
architecture is based on two complementary ideas. The first is
SSAM
, an attention mechanism that learns to focus on important events and suppress insignificant ones. It is like an experienced trader who can discern market sentiment behind the flow of candlestick patterns — where momentum is full of energy and where it is merely a fading wave. The second is
STFS
(
Spatiotemporal Feature Sampling Strategy
). It broadens the model’s perception, allowing it to see a smooth sequence of interconnected events.
To draw an analogy,
SSAM
is a trader’s attention, and
STFS
is the trader’s memory. Together, they form a model that can notice and remember what happened before. This is the true essence of analysis: not getting stuck in the moment, while also not losing touch with the context.
When we transfer these ideas into the
MQL5
environment, the challenge becomes not only technical but also philosophical. A video camera records changes in brightness, while the market captures changes in the state of price and volume. Every tick, every spike in volatility, every change in the order book — all of these can become a
spike
if the significance criterion is defined correctly.
This approach makes you look at the market differently. We see a system of impulses from which a macro-movement is formed.
S3CE-Net
seems to translate market speech into the language of events, where each change is a letter and the entire series is a sentence. The model learns to read this language the way an experienced analyst reads a tape chart: not with their eyes, but by intuition.
S3CE-Net
does not wait for a pattern to be confirmed — it reacts to precursors. This is especially important in highly volatile markets, where traditional indicators lag behind.
To a trader who is used to relying on candlestick patterns or indicators, this idea may seem unfamiliar. But if you look more closely, it is a logical continuation of the evolution of analysis. First, we assessed levels and zones; then we moved on to probabilistic models; now it is time for event-driven models. It is a natural progression — from observation to understanding, from data to meaning.
That is precisely why the work on implementing
S3CE-Net
using
MQL5
is not limited to purely technical goals. We aim to show how architectural principles developed for a completely different field can breathe new life into market analysis. After all, both trading and event-driven analytics are about searching for structure in chaos — the ability to extract meaning from the flow.
The market, like any living system, breathes unevenly, and whoever can hear this rhythm gains an advantage.
S3CE-Net
is an attempt to give machines this sense of hearing — to enable an algorithm to sense where movement begins and where it ends. This is not magic — it is the result of a careful analysis of the structure of events.
The author’s visualization of the S3CE-Net framework is shown below.
Today we are approaching the logical conclusion. The architecture, implementation, and adaptation are now behind us. Ahead lie testing, evaluation, and, perhaps, a rethinking of our usual approach to forecasting. We will see how well the model we have built handles real-world market flows, how accurately it distinguishes genuine signals, and how its
spike-guided
attention affects the quality of its forecasts.
STFS Module
Today, we have one final step left to take in implementing the approaches proposed by the authors of the
S3CE-Net
framework: to build the
STFS
(
Spatio-Temporal Feature Sampling Strategy
) module. This is the final component of the entire architecture, capable of teaching the model to view the market holistically — to perceive the broader context rather than becoming fixated on local patterns.
Like any experienced trader,
STFS
learns to distinguish what matters from what is secondary. Its task is to make the model analyze not only specific segments of market data, but also the relationships between them, combining the perception of time and space. After all, the market is not just a line on a chart. It is a multidimensional system in which every candle, every volume reading, and every impulse are linked by invisible threads. It is precisely these connections that the algorithm must learn to recognize.
The authors of
S3CE-Net
proposed a very elegant mechanism for this. During training, the module divides the feature map into subsamples along the time and spatial dimensions.
First,
temporal sampling
is performed. A set of time steps is randomly selected from the entire sequence. For each of them, an averaged representation is calculated — a kind of
snapshot of the market state
at a specific moment. These snapshots form a set of temporal features that reflect the dynamics of the process.
Next comes
spatial sampling
. The feature map is divided into several random regions. Each region is averaged separately, which makes it possible to identify local structures. If we draw an analogy with the market, this is similar to analyzing different sectors of market activity.
Finally, at the last stage,
a global semantic vector
is extracted, representing a generalized view of the entire market state. It is created by averaging the entire feature map and serves as an aggregate indicator that synthesizes both temporal and spatial patterns.
The model's training relies on two key loss functions:
triplet loss
and
cross-entropy with label smoothing
. The first helps the model identify key features by amplifying the differences between truly significant market states. The second stabilizes training by preventing the model from overestimating random fluctuations. Together, they give the system the
intuition
that allows it not to get lost in market noise.
In this article, we will take the liberty of slightly reinterpreting the original approach proposed by the authors of
S3CE-Net
. While the original concept focused primarily on analyzing the spatiotemporal structure of an image, the nature of the signal being analyzed is different in the case of financial data. The market has no geometry — its structure is not visual but semantic. Here, the features constitute a vector of economic factors, where each coordinate carries its own context: price, volume, volatility, sentiment indicators, and structural liquidity metrics. And, most importantly, their interrelationships do not necessarily correlate with the proximity of their indices in this vector.
That is precisely why the direct application of spatial sampling, as in the classical
STFS
implementation for images, is not always justified. We cannot assume that adjacent elements in a feature vector have similar values or effects. In market data,
neighborhood
is
defined by functional relationships
. Price may be closely related to volume, but not at all to a technical indicator occupying the neighboring index in the data array.
For this reason, we use a reinterpreted sampling strategy similar to temporal sampling, but applied to the spatial (
feature
) axis. In other words, just as we select random time points in temporal sampling, here we will randomly select a subset of features to form a training sample for the model. This approach preserves the idea of randomness and generalization, but makes it relevant specifically to vector market data, where meaning — rather than location — is key.
Furthermore, unlike the original method — in which data not included in the sample are simply discarded — we will take a different approach. Not a single feature will be lost. From the remaining data, we will create
alternative samples
that will be used as supplementary contexts. This not only improves the effectiveness of training but also enhances the model’s robustness — it learns to view the market from different angles, as if analyzing it through a set of independent yet consistent observations.
As a result, five different representations of the analyzed data are generated:
full
(
global
), reflecting the overall market environment;
2 samples
— temporal and feature-based, providing local focus for the model;
2 alternative samples
that serve as additional sources for contextual learning.
We are also making changes to the way we generate the final forecast. In the classic
STFS
version for images, the features of the selected blocks are averaged, after which a single vector is formed. When applied to market data, this approach can smooth out important signals, causing subtle but significant impulses to be lost.
That is why we take a different approach: we generate a separate forecast for each of the samples obtained. In other words, the model does not combine information in advance, but analyzes each perspective separately. This makes it possible to evaluate signals in different contexts without losing the local significance of the data and while retaining the ability to distinguish weak but potentially important trends.
This approach is similar to the analytical style of a professional trader. An experienced trader never relies on a single indicator or a single time interval: they build several scenarios at once, compare them with one another, and use this basis to make a decision about the position. Similarly, our model learns to generate multiple forecasts based on the same information, viewing the market from different perspectives.
Now that the design concept for the
STFS
module has been defined and refined, it is time to move on to its practical implementation. The first step is to form five representations of the data being analyzed. To create all samples efficiently and in parallel, we use the
OpenCL
context, which allows us to process data arrays simultaneously and significantly speeds up the calculations.
The implementation is based on the
STFS
kernel, which creates subsamples using random masks of time steps and features. Each data point is checked for data validity, after which all necessary sample combinations are generated. This approach allows us to create both the main and alternative samples simultaneously, without waiting for sequential processing, which is critical when working with streaming market data.

Thus, the kernel’s output is a complete set of five representations of the input data, ready for the subsequent generation of individual forecasts. This is a key aspect of the practical implementation of
STFS
: the model is able to learn simultaneously from different
eyes of the market
, viewing it both globally and locally, as well as through alternative lenses.
It is worth noting that the kernel algorithm for distributing error gradients is based on similar logic. We suggest leaving the implementation details of this mechanism for independent study. The complete code for the OpenCL program is included in the attachment.

The class structure reflects the key components of
STFS
: separate objects for temporal and feature masks (
cMaskTime
,
cMaskSpatial
), a tensor for merging representations (
cConcatenated
), and specialized convolutional and transpose layers (
cSpatialDScale
,
cTimeDScale
,
caTranspose

a platform
that enables the model to account for various aspects of market information simultaneously and generate five forecast values derived from different representations.
All internal components of the
CNeuronSTFS
class are declared statically, allowing the constructor and destructor to be left empty. The object is created and initialized entirely within the
Init
method. This approach simplifies memory management and ensures predictable initialization of all parts of the module.

The
Init
method performs sequential configuration of each internal component of the
STFS
module. First, the base initialization of the parent class is called, after which no activation is set on the main object.
It is particularly important to note here that the absence of an activation function at the module level is a prerequisite for the algorithm to function correctly. The authors of the
S3CE-Net
framework recommend using the
STFS
module only during the training phase. In production deployment, when the system generates forecasts in real time, only the complete data representation is used, without creating subsamples. Therefore, as will be shown below, the module returns only the forecast based on the complete representation, while all intermediate subsamples serve solely to strengthen the training process and build a more robust and accurate model. However, within the module, a parallel subsample training process is built, and to propagate gradients correctly across all components of the module,
the raw error
is required, without any adjustments for the derivative of the activation function.
At the same time, for flexibility depending on the user's needs, activation may still be used functionally, but it is moved to the last data projection object. It is there, when obtaining the final forecast, that a nonlinear transformation can be applied if required for a specific model operating scenario.
But let's return to the initialization algorithm. Next, masks for temporal sampling and feature sampling are created and configured. Each one is assigned its own index.

All components are configured to perform parallel computations on the
OpenCL

The forward-pass algorithm is implemented in the
feedForward
method. Its task is to pass the data step by step through all the module components in order to obtain a ready-to-use representation for the forecast.

(!STFS(NeuronOCL))
return

First, the
STFS

In it, unlike the familiar methods for queuing kernels for execution, the masks of the temporal steps and the analyzed features are sampled first. Only after the preparatory work has been completed is control passed to the corresponding kernel.
After that, the data passes through a convolutional layer for projecting spatial features, allowing the model to identify local structures and relationships between features in different representations.

false

Thus, the
feedForward
method ensures a smooth flow of data through the entire
STFS

Once the model has generated predicted values, the
error-correction
stage begins — backpropagation of gradients. The
calcInputGradients
method is responsible for distributing the error among all components of the
STFS
module in accordance with their influence on the final result.

(!NeuronOCL)

It is important to note here that the
STFS

At the same time, different data projections — global, temporal, feature-based, and alternative samples — have different errors. To train each projection correctly, it is preferable to have
target values
rather than deviations. To obtain these target values, the module’s prediction results are summed with the incoming error, forming a tensor that can be used to train individual projections correctly.
That is precisely why the absence of an activation function at the module's output becomes critically important. Any nonlinear transformation would distort this process, and the network would lose its ability to correctly distribute errors and generate accurate target values for each projection.

It is precisely thanks to this mechanism that the model learns to identify and distinguish between global and local market patterns, thereby developing a robust and accurate forecasting model.
In practical terms, for a trader, this means that every element of the module, from subsamples to convolutional blocks, receives feedback on its significance for the final forecast, which improves the quality of training and enables the model to effectively handle noisy and volatile market data.
The complete code for the class and all of its methods is provided in the attachment.
Model Architecture
Now that all the key modules of the framework have been implemented, we move on to the next stage — describing the model architecture. Following the approach of the authors of
S3CE-Net
, we use the
Environment State Encoder
model from
SEW-ResNeXt
, which has proven effective at extracting meaningful features from streaming data.
Within this architecture, we introduce
SSAM blocks
that provide selective attention to the most informative features and their combinations. This approach allows the network to focus on key market signals while minimizing the impact of noise and random fluctuations, which is particularly important for highly volatile financial data.
To avoid overloading the article and to keep it readable, we do not include the full
Encoder
diagram. Details of the architecture are available in the attachment to the article, where each layer and block is described in detail. Readers can review the targeted changes to the architecture and the complete structure on their own.
It should be noted in particular that the
STFS
module is used exclusively during the training phase. In live deployment, when the model generates real-time forecasts, subsamples and separate data projections are unnecessary, and generating them only increases the load on system resources. To use computing resources efficiently, we have moved
STFS
into a separate model that is used only for training.
The model begins by creating the
input data layer
, which corresponds to the features being analyzed and the observation window.

Separating
STFS
into a standalone model allows for the separation of training and production use, reducing the load on the real-time system while fully preserving the benefits of parallel training across different market projections.
As for the architecture of the
Actor
and
Critic
models, it has been carried over entirely from our previous work. This makes it possible to retain time-tested solutions for generating actions and evaluating their quality. It also makes it possible to integrate new components without compromising training stability. The result is a full-fledged model that combines both traditional approaches to managing a market strategy and modern methods for identifying significant features and making robust forecasts.
Testing
We have completed a major effort to integrate all the key components of the framework, and now it is time to evaluate the effectiveness of the solutions we have implemented. But first, the strategy must be trained and thoroughly tested using historical and simulated data, much like honing the skills of an experienced trader and verifying the algorithm’s ability to perform under a wide variety of market conditions.
We will conduct the first stage — offline training — using historical data for the
EURUSD
currency pair on the
H1
timeframe for the period from
January 2024
to
June 2025
. This period served as a sort of training ground. The model learned to recognize historical patterns, understand price dynamics and trading volumes, identify relationships between key features, and use them in forecasts. Thanks to the
STFS
module, it simultaneously mastered global and local data representations, forming five different projections, which improved the accuracy and robustness of the forecasts. It could be said that the model developed
trader’s intuition
, combined with the mathematical rigor of data analysis.
The next stage — online fine-tuning in the MetaTrader 5 Strategy Tester — enabled the model to work with real-time data streams. Here, it mastered the dynamics of a live market, learned to maintain stability amid market noise, adjust its actions in low-liquidity conditions, and react instantly to sharp price spikes. SSAM blocks kept the focus on the most informative features, even when the data were unstable.
The final test was conducted using data from
July through September 2025
, which were entirely new and had not been used previously. All parameters obtained in the previous stages were loaded without modification, which ensured a fair assessment of the model's generalization ability. The results confirm that a step-by-step approach to training and adaptation, using
STFS
and
SSAM
, enables the model to analyze the market and generate forecasts of key market features that traders can rely on when making actual trading decisions.
The results of the model testing demonstrate high stability and accuracy in the forecasts. The account balance showed steady growth from an initial deposit of USD 100 to USD 108.75, while equity smoothly tracked the balance, indicating that the forecast allocation and risk management mechanism was working correctly.
The maximum balance drawdown was only 2.07%, while the maximum equity drawdown was 4.51%, indicating a low level of risk and the strategy's resilience even amid market fluctuations. The overall profit factor is
2.60
, which confirms the model's ability to effectively select profitable signals.
In terms of trade structure, 8 out of 16 trades were profitable, representing a
50%
success rate, and the average profitable trade was
1.78
, while the average loss was limited to
0.69
, demonstrating a good balance between return and risk. The largest profit on a single trade reached
5.02
, while the largest loss was limited to
1.99
, which also confirms the model's prudence in capital management.
The model combining
SSAM
and
STFS
demonstrated modest, low-profile capital growth with a small drawdown and a good risk-reward ratio. The result is promising, but so far statistically limited. Before moving the strategy into live trading, more extensive tests and stress tests must be conducted to confirm the stability of its behavior over long and challenging market periods.
Conclusion
We went all the way from an idea to a working tool, doing it as if we were assembling a precise clockwork mechanism — carefully, step by step, and with attention to detail.
Using
MQL5
, we implemented the key components of
S3CE-Net
:
implemented
SSAM
into the
SEW-ResNeXt
encoder,
adapted
STFS
for a market feature vector,
prepared an
OpenCL
kernel for the parallel generation of five representations.
The key engineering idea is the separation of modes.
STFS
works effectively, but its place is during training. In production, we keep only the global representation. This conserves resources and ensures predictable behavior. A practical detail that is important to keep in mind: the absence of activation within the module is not a matter of preference, but a requirement for correctly forming target tensors and propagating gradients between projections.
Tests conducted on EURUSD H1 for July–September 2025 showed promising results. The model takes a conservative approach. All of this provides a solid foundation, but it does not lock the strategy in for life.
What traders need to understand: current metrics are encouraging, but the sample size is small. High results based on a small sample can be misleading. Our task now is not to celebrate victory, but to test its robustness.

for: STFS module generates five different representations of the data: full (global), 2 samples (temporal and feature-based), and 2 alternative samples — enabling multi-perspective analysis analogous to a professional trader building several scenarios

The model generates a separate forecast for each of the five samples, preserving local significance and avoiding signal smoothing — unlike classical averaging that risks losing subtle but significant impulses

Training uses triplet loss (to amplify differences between truly significant market states) and cross-entropy with label smoothing (to prevent overestimation of random fluctuations), directly targeting robust signal discrimination
Testing was conducted on out-of-sample EURUSD H1 data from July–September 2025 — entirely new and unused in training — to assess generalization ability

Results show maximum equity drawdown of 4.51%, profit factor of 2.60, 50% win rate, and average profit/loss ratio of 1.78 / 0.69 — quantifiable, historical performance metrics derived from real backtesting

against: The article describes a neural network architecture (S3CE-Net) with SSAM and STFS modules, but provides no explicit, deterministic trading signal rule — e.g., no condition like 'enter long when STFS output > X and SSAM attention score on volume spike exceeds Y'. Instead, it only gives high-level architectural descriptions ('the model learns to sense where movement begins'), training strategies (triplet loss, label smoothing), and implementation details (OpenCL kernels, class structures). No formulaic entry/exit logic is stated.

The model relies on 'spike'-based event detection, defined via 'significance criterion' (e.g., 'every tick, every spike in volatility, every change in the order book — all of these can become a spike if the significance criterion is defined correctly'), but the criterion itself is never specified — neither mathematically nor operationally. This makes the core signal generation mechanism undefined and non-reproducible from the text.

The architecture uses 'structural liquidity metrics', 'sentiment indicators', and 'order book changes' as input features. These are not available in standard spot Forex: structural liquidity metrics require order-book depth (Level 2/3 data), sentiment indicators imply external NLP or news feeds, and 'changes in the order book' explicitly require exchange-level market depth — none of which exist for retail spot Forex brokers.

The STFS module generates five representations (global, temporal sample, feature sample, and two alternatives) and 'generates a separate forecast for each', then — in production — uses *only the global representation*. However, the article states that 'all intermediate subsamples serve solely to strengthen the training process' and that 'in live deployment [...] only the complete data representation is used'. Crucially, the *trading decision is never linked to any output of the model*: no mapping from forecast(s) → trade direction/size/entry is given. The testing section reports equity curves and trade stats, but does not specify how those trades were generated from model outputs — i.e., the decision policy (e.g., thresholding, voting, RL action mapping) is absent.
non_fatal: No out-of-sample test details beyond date ranges are provided (e.g., walk-forward protocol, train/validation/test split ratios).
No mention of spread, slippage, or commission modeling in testing — though the article explicitly excludes these from fatal assessment.
The reported test period (July–Sept 2025) is future-dated relative to the article’s YEAR=2026, suggesting possible hindsight bias or synthetic data — but per instructions, this is non-fatal.
The model uses OpenCL acceleration and MQL5-specific classes (e.g., CNeuronSTFS), implying platform lock-in — but infrastructure dependency is non-fatal per criteria (5).

judge.reject_reason: Статья описывает архитектуру нейросетевой модели S3CE-Net (с модулями SSAM и STFS), её реализацию в MQL5 и OpenCL, а также общие результаты тестирования, но не содержит чёткого, детерминированного правила входа: нет ни математической формулы, ни логического условия (например, 'вход в лонг при значении выхода STFS > X и одновременном превышении SSAM-внимания на волатильность порога Y'), ни определения критерия 'спайка' — он объявлен необходимым, но не задан. Также отсутствует любая спецификация того, как именно выход модели преобразуется в торговый сигнал (пороги, голосование, RL-политика и т.п.). Входные данные включают недоступные в розничном спот-форексе элементы: структурные метрики ликвидности, данные стакана (Level 2/3), индикаторы сентимента — что делает правило неприменимым на закрытых барах спот-форекса. Это фатальные пороки: невозможность записать правило и использование неприменимых данных.
judge.formula_and_logic: не указано — статья не содержит формулы или логики генерации торгового сигнала; описаны только архитектурные компоненты (STFS, SSAM), методы обучения (triplet loss, label smoothing) и общий принцип 'обнаружения спайков', но без определения спайка, без связи выхода модели с направлением сделки и без порогов/условий входа.
judge.author_oos_metrics: Тест на вне-выборочных данных EURUSD H1 за июль–сентябрь 2025 показал рост баланса с 100 до 108.75 USD, максимальный просадок баланса 2.07%, просадок эквити 4.51%, коэффициент прибыли 2.60, 50% прибыльных сделок, средняя прибыль 1.78, средний убыток 0.69.
judge.summary: Статья представляет нейросетевую архитектуру S3CE-Net для обнаружения рыночных 'спайков' через модули SSAM и STFS, реализованную в MQL5 с использованием OpenCL. Автор демонстрирует её обучение и тестирование на EURUSD H1, сообщая о консервативных, но положительных результатах на вне-выборочных данных за июль–сентябрь 2025.
